extracted.intended_audience: public company general counsel, investor relations teams, corporate secretaries and compliance officers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical legal and governance guidance for building and maintaining a public company's investor relations (IR) website to satisfy SEC rules and stock exchange listing requirements and to support Regulation FD/G and investor communications. Focuses on what documents/information to post, timing, archival practices, third-party content, social media and periodic review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Website requirements at the time of the IPO
rubrics_metrics.description: NYSE requires listed companies to post certain governance documents on their corporate websites by the earlier of the IPO closing date or five business days from the listing date: audit committee charter; compensation committee charter; nominating/corporate governance committee charter; corporate governance guidelines; code of business conduct and ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an NYSE-listed company opts to make additional specified information available on its website instead of in its SEC filings (e.g., name of presiding director, method for communicating with presiding director/independent directors, audit committee member’s simultaneous service disclosures), the company must disclose that fact in its annual proxy statement or Form 10-K and provide its website address therein. Nasdaq does not impose the same comprehensive requirement at IPO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nasdaq posting and proxy-appendix rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Nasdaq-listed companies are required to make their code of conduct publicly available and posting it on a corporate website satisfies this requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a Nasdaq-listed company does not post the charters of its audit, compensation and nominating/corporate governance committees (or committees performing similar functions) to its website, the SEC requires it to include copies of those charters as appendices to its proxy statement at least once every three years.

rubrics_metrics.name: SEC website disclosures for code of ethics and director independence definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A company must disclose in its Form 10-K whether it has adopted a code of ethics for certain senior officers and, if so, must make it publicly available on its website, file it as an exhibit to Form 10-K, or indicate how to request a free copy. If a company uses its own director independence definitions (rather than exchange rules), it must disclose in its proxy whether it has provided these definitions on its website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make code of ethics and director independence definitions easily accessible and document where they are posted and how they can be requested; consider filing or hyperlinking as applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post periodic and current reports on the website promptly after filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies that are accelerated filers and large accelerated filers must post their annual, quarterly and current Exchange Act reports on their corporate websites as soon as reasonably practicable after such reports are filed or furnished with the SEC, or explain in their annual reports why they do not do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SEC recommends keeping periodic and current reports posted for at least 12 months; many companies maintain longer archives. NYSE-listed companies required to file Form 10-K must simultaneously make such reports available on or through their websites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post annual proxy statements and shareholder annual reports on the website
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies required to deliver proxy materials must also post proxy materials (including the annual report to shareholders) on a publicly accessible website and provide shareholders with a notice in the proxy statement indicating where the materials may be accessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies may satisfy the obligation to provide the SEC with copies of annual reports sent to shareholders by posting them to their websites if the report remains accessible for at least one year after posting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post Section 16 beneficial ownership reports by end of business day
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies must post all beneficial ownership reports filed by officers, directors and >10% beneficial owners by the end of the business day after each form is filed with the SEC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports may be posted directly or via hyperlink to EDGAR or a third-party service; each report must remain accessible for at least 12 months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely disclose amendments and waivers to required codes of ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: The SEC requires public disclosure of amendments to or waivers of a company’s SEC-required code of ethics for certain senior officers either by (1) posting the information on the company’s website within four business days after the amendment or waiver (provided the company has disclosed its website address and intention to use it in its most recent Form 10-K), or (2) filing a Form 8-K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any amendment or waiver disclosed on the website must remain posted for at least 12 months; ensure the company has properly elected and disclosed the website-as-disclosure-channel approach in its 10‑K before relying on this route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party director compensation disclosure (Nasdaq)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Nasdaq-listed company must publicly disclose on its website, or in the proxy/information statement for the next shareholder meeting, the material terms of all agreements/arrangements between any director or nominee and any third party relating to compensation or other payment connected to that person’s candidacy or service as a director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NYE does not have a similar requirement; ensure Nasdaq-specific disclosures are posted timely and are complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of contributions to tax-exempt organizations (NYSE)
rubrics_metrics.description: An NYSE-listed company can satisfy disclosure obligations regarding certain contributions to tax-exempt organizations (in which independent directors serve as executives) on or through its corporate website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post material terms and context so investors can assess potential conflicts of interest; clearly date and contextualize such disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict minerals disclosure and related website disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: A company that depends on conflict minerals for the functionality or production of a product must file a Form SD and make certain related website disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor evolving scope of conflict minerals obligations; ensure web disclosures align with filed Form SD and are easy to locate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish delisting notices on website and by press release contemporaneously
rubrics_metrics.description: If a public company intends to withdraw a class of securities from listing or registration under Section 12(b), it must publish a notice of its intent with reasons on its website and via a press release, contemporaneously with written notice to the exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear, dated notice and rationale; coordinate timing with exchanges and press release distribution to avoid gaps in disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with XBRL interactive data rules
rubrics_metrics.description: As of September 17, 2018 the SEC no longer requires issuers to post interactive data XBRL files to their corporate websites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Update IR practices to reflect current SEC XBRL requirements; continue to consider investor needs for accessible financial data even if posting XBRL is not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post additional corporate governance materials as a best practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond required items, many companies post other materials to enhance governance transparency and investor relations, including: certificate/articles of incorporation and bylaws; list of directors and senior management with bios/photos; list of board committees with members/chairs and purposes; environmental and social policy information; director attendance at meetings; lead director charter; policy on board oversight of political spending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider this non-exhaustive list to improve investor perception and provide a comprehensive governance profile; ensure any such materials are current, dated and consistent with filed disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the website as part of Regulation FD communications when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: A corporate website can be a ‘recognized channel of distribution’ for Regulation FD purposes if the company identifies the website in periodic and other reports as a place where it routinely posts important information and establishes a pattern and practice of posting such information there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about relying solely on the website; consider market pickup and reporting, and document the pattern of use. Often combine website posting with Form 8‑K or press release to ensure broad, non-exclusionary distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earnings releases, webcasts and investor decks disclosure practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The SEC recommends announcing webcasts/earnings calls through a Regulation FD-compliant disclosure at least a few days prior to the event, including date/time/subject matter/call-in info, and making replays available for a reasonable time. Supplemental materials (e.g., presentation slides) should be posted and companies should state how/for how long transcripts or replays will be available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many companies issue a press release to announce webcasts and post materials on their websites; supplemental materials referenced in webcasts should be disclosed in the announcement to help establish that they have been made public in a Regulation FD-compliant manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation G compliance for non-GAAP financial measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation G requires that public disclosure of material non-GAAP financial measures be accompanied by a presentation of, and reconciliation to, the most directly comparable GAAP measure. If presented orally (e.g., webcast), the required reconciliation may be provided by posting it on the company’s website and disclosing its location during the presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure reconciliations are posted and remain available (SEC recommends at least 12 months); treat website postings of non-GAAP reconciliations with the same care as other SEC disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperlinking to or providing third-party content — liability and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A public company is responsible—and potentially liable—for all content posted on its corporate website, and may be liable for third-party content on its site or linked from it if a reasonable person would infer company approval or endorsement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid placing third-party hyperlinks in the same section or with the same style as company-provided content; provide clear disclaimers (often click-through) that the company does not approve/endorse third-party content and does not monitor it. Understand that disclaimers do not fully absolve liability, particularly if the company knows or is reckless regarding materially false or misleading third-party content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date posts and archive old information clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Information posted should be clearly dated and identified as historical or archived once it is no longer current; the SEC has clarified that access to prior materials does not mean they have been republished or reissued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain separate sections for 'upcoming,' 'recent' and 'historical' investor presentations and date all material (including webcasts and related info) to avoid investor confusion or perceived duty to update older materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodically review the website for currency and compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies should schedule regularly recurring reviews of their investor relations websites to ensure all information and materials remain current and compliant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In-house legal and investor relations teams should update the website whenever governance materials are revised or there are changes to management, the board or committee composition; document review schedules and updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a dedicated annual shareholder meeting webpage
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider creating a dedicated webpage for the annual shareholder meeting that provides all related content in one user-friendly place and can present annual reports and proxy disclosures in more interactive formats and supplemental multimedia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplemental material posted on such pages may need to be filed as 'additional soliciting material' under Rule 14a-6(b). Optimize content for multiple platforms, encourage access in proxy materials and promote the page on homepages and social media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions for controlled companies and foreign private issuers
rubrics_metrics.description: Controlled companies (more than 50% voting power held by a person/group) are not required to have certain committees and thus need not post those committee charters on their websites while controlled. Foreign private issuers may follow home country practices in lieu of U.S. exchange listing rules, but must disclose significant differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign private issuers have SEC exemptions from Section 16 reports, Form 8‑K and SEC-compliant proxy statements unless they elect to follow U.S. forms; they are generally not required to post Forms 20‑F or 40‑F. Nevertheless, certain code-of-ethics provisions and public disclosures (via Form 6‑K or website) may still apply. Review exchange rules and SEC cross-border exceptions carefully to determine what to post.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media channels and Regulation FD compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: The SEC’s framework for the corporate website as a recognized channel of distribution similarly applies to social media. Companies should disclose in periodic reports the social media channels they intend to use for disclosures, consider whether those channels will be considered public based on followers/traffic, and if not recognized channels, disclose material non-public information through them only after or in connection with Regulation FD-compliant disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train social media users (including executives) on Regulation FD practices and have knowledgeable counsel or IR staff monitor social posts for inadvertent disclosures of material non-public information. Analyze follower counts and traffic when deciding whether a social channel can be relied upon as a recognized distribution channel.
